pages.text: The Talent Show

image.note: Cover: shadow animals on a wall, a lamp, a small boy

pages.text: Contents. The Secret on the Wall / Signed Up / Stage Fright / The Rehearsal Disaster / The Night / The Shadows.

The lion prowled across the wall, huge and dark, opened its jaws, and roared, silently. Then it melted into a bird, which flew, which became a fish, which became a whole ship sailing a shadow sea. And all of it, every shape, was made by Boma's two hands in the light of one lamp, alone in his room, where nobody could see.

image.note: Boma making shadow shapes on his bedroom wall

pages.text: Boma was the quietest boy on the estate. In a crowd he shrank; if a teacher asked his name he went hot and stared at his shoes. But alone, in the lamplight, his hands could do the most astonishing things: fold and turn and become any creature you could dream, thrown huge and alive upon the wall.

image.note: Shy Boma in class, staring down at his desk

pages.text: He had taught himself, over many quiet evenings, one shape at a time. A dog. A rabbit. An eagle with beating wings. It was his own secret magic, and he had never shown a single soul, because showing meant being seen, and being seen was the one thing Boma could not bear.

image.note: Boma practising a shadow eagle at night

pages.text: So when the notice went up, TAFIYA ESTATE TALENT SHOW, SATURDAY, hosted by Mrs Obi, with a real stage and real lights, Boma read it, felt his stomach turn over, and walked quickly away. A stage. Lights. A whole crowd, watching. Not for him. Never for him.

image.note: Boma hurrying past the talent show notice

pages.text: But Boma had a friend named Emeka, loud where Boma was quiet, bold where Boma was shy, and Emeka had once, by accident, seen the shadows on the wall through a gap in the curtain. He had never forgotten them. "They were the best thing I ever saw," he said. "Everyone should see them."

image.note: Emeka peeking through a curtain gap, amazed

pages.text: So Emeka did a terrible, wonderful thing. He put Boma's name down for the talent show. Without asking. When Boma found out, he went white, then hot, then nearly ran all the way to the gate. "You had no right!" he cried. "I can't! I can't stand up there! Take it off, take my name off now!"

image.note: Boma horrified, Emeka guilty, the sign-up sheet

pages.text: "I can't take it off," said Emeka, which was not quite true, but he believed the shadows were worth it. "Boma. You have something nobody else has. It is a crime to hide it in a bedroom. Just this once. I will be right there. I promise." Boma did not answer. But he did not, quite, say no.

image.note: Emeka pleading, Boma silent and torn

pages.text: The week that followed was the worst of Boma's life. Every time he thought of the stage, his hands, his clever, magic hands, turned cold and clumsy and would not make a single shape. Fear had stolen the one thing he was good at. "You see?" he told Emeka miserably. "I will freeze. I will ruin it. I told you."

image.note: Boma's hands trembling, no shadow forming

pages.text: Mrs Obi, who missed nothing, drew him aside. "I hear you make shadows," she said gently. Boma nodded at the floor. "And you are afraid of the crowd." He nodded again. "Then here is a secret," she said. "When the shadows play, the lights go down. The crowd cannot see you at all. They will see only the magic. You will be there in the dark, quite hidden, just as you like."

image.note: Mrs Obi speaking kindly to Boma

pages.text: Hidden. In the dark. Only the shadows in the light. Something in Boma unlocked, just a little. Perhaps, if no one could see him, if it was only his hands and the wall, the way it always was, perhaps, just perhaps, he could.

image.note: Boma considering, a small flicker of hope

pages.text: At the rehearsal, it nearly ended before it began. The other acts went first: Grema thundered on his drums, a girl sang, two boys told jokes. Then came Boma's turn, and as he stepped near the stage, someone tripped over the lamp cord and the light crashed to the floor and went dark. No lamp, no light, no shadows. Boma's act was, it seemed, impossible.

image.note: The fallen lamp, Boma dismayed backstage

pages.text: Everyone groaned. The talent show was tomorrow. Where would they find another lamp bright and steady enough by then? Boma, strangely, did not run. For the first time, it was not his own fear that filled him, but a problem to solve, and problems, unlike crowds, did not frighten him at all.

image.note: The broken lamp, the group worried, Boma thinking

pages.text: "A phone," said Boma quietly. Everyone turned, surprised to hear him speak at all. "A phone torch. It is small, and bright, and steady, and it never flickers. If someone holds it just so, behind me..." Mrs Obi smiled. "Then we shall light your shadows with a phone," she said. Emeka whooped. The show was saved, and Boma had saved it.

image.note: Boma suggesting the phone torch, faces brightening

pages.text: On the night, the community room was full, every chair taken, the lights bright and warm. Boma sat backstage with his cold hands in his lap, and all his courage drained away again. "I can't," he whispered. "Emeka, I really can't." And Emeka, for once, said nothing clever. He just sat beside him, and held his shoulder, and waited.

image.note: Boma backstage, Emeka's hand on his shoulder

pages.text: One by one the acts went by, to claps and cheers, and each one made Boma's dread grow heavier. Then Mrs Obi's voice rang out. "And now, something you have never seen before. Lights, please, all the way down." And the room went dark. Completely dark. And in the dark, Boma could not be seen at all.

image.note: The room going dark, Boma stepping out unseen

pages.text: In the dark, Emeka switched on the phone torch. A single beam. A blank white wall. And two hands, Boma's hands, rising into the light, no longer cold, no longer clumsy, but sure and quick and magic, just as they always were, alone, in his room, where nobody could see.

image.note: The torch beam, Boma's hands rising into the light

pages.text: And then the wall came alive. A bird flew across it, so real the crowd gasped. It became a galloping horse. A great elephant raised its trunk. A tiny mouse scampered, chased by a shadow cat, and the children shrieked with delight. A whole silent story unfolded on the wall, and the room forgot to breathe.

image.note: The wall alive with shadow animals, crowd amazed

pages.text: Nobody could see the boy who made it. That was the secret of it. They saw only the magic, floating free in the dark, a lion, a ship, a flock of birds rising, and they clapped and laughed and gasped as though the wall itself were dreaming. And in the dark behind the light, Boma smiled, for the first time on any stage.

image.note: The crowd delighted, Boma smiling unseen behind the light

pages.text: When the last shadow, a great bird, spread its wings and flew away into nothing, and the lights came slowly up, the whole room rose to its feet. And there, blinking in the brightness, small and shy and quite astonished, stood Boma, the quietest boy on the estate, getting the loudest cheer of the night.

image.note: Lights up, Boma revealed, the room on its feet

pages.text: He did not run. He stood, and went hot, and then, slowly, he smiled, and gave one small bow. Emeka was cheering loudest of all. "I told you," Emeka shouted over the noise. "I told you it was a crime to hide it." And Boma, for the first time, thought perhaps his loud, impossible friend had been right.

image.note: Boma taking a small bow, Emeka cheering

pages.text: Boma did not suddenly become loud, or bold, or unafraid. He was still the quiet boy, the next day and ever after. But now, when the estate children begged, "Boma, do the shadows!", he would fetch a torch, and find a wall, and let his hands do the talking, which had always, all along, been his way of being seen.

image.note: Boma happily making shadows for a small group of kids

pages.text: The Talent Show. Boma, whose hands make magic in the dark. Emeka, the friend who would not let him hide. Mrs Obi, who knew that some stars shine best with the lights down low. A reminder: being quiet is not the same as having nothing to show.

image.note: Boma and Emeka, a shadow bird on the wall behind
